Name: Existentialism
Description: Philosophy emphasizing individual existence, freedom, choice, and the search for meaning in an absurd universe.
CorePrinciples: Existence precedes essence
Radical freedom and responsibility
Authenticity: living according to one's own values
Angst and the confrontation with nothingness
Absurdity of existence
Individual must create own meaning
Bad faith: self-deception about one's freedom

Name: Pragmatism
Description: Philosophy that evaluates theories and beliefs by their practical consequences and usefulness.
Sources: How to Make Our Ideas Clear (Charles Sanders Peirce)
CorePrinciples: Truth is what works in practice
Meaning comes from practical consequences
Anti-foundationalism: no absolute truths
Experimental method in philosophy
Context-dependent knowledge
Fallibilism: all beliefs are provisional
Problem-solving orientation

Name: Utilitarianism
Description: Ethical theory that the right action is that which maximizes overall happiness or well-being.
Sources: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (Jeremy Bentham)
CorePrinciples: Greatest happiness principle: maximize utility
Consequentialism: outcomes determine morality
Impartial consideration of all affected parties
Hedonism: pleasure is good, pain is bad
Calculation of costs and benefits
Individual rights may be overridden for greater good
Progressive social reform

Name: Kantian Ethics (Deontology)
Description: Ethical theory emphasizing duty, universal moral laws, and treating persons as ends in themselves.
Sources: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (Immanuel Kant)
CorePrinciples: Categorical Imperative: act only on maxims you could will to be universal laws
Persons are ends in themselves, never mere means
Duty and moral law over consequences
Autonomy and rational agency
Good will is the only unconditional good
Universal human dignity
Moral duties are absolute, not conditional

Name: Virtue Ethics (Aristotelian)
Description: Ethical theory focused on character, virtues, and human flourishing rather than rules or consequences.
CorePrinciples: Eudaimonia: human flourishing as the highest good
Virtues as character excellences
Golden mean: virtue lies between extremes
Practical wisdom (phronesis) guides action
Character developed through habituation
Teleological: humans have natural purpose
Community and relationships essential for ethics

Name: Rationalism (Cartesian)
Description: Epistemological position that reason and innate ideas are the primary sources of knowledge.
CorePrinciples: Reason as primary source of knowledge
A priori knowledge independent of experience
Innate ideas exist in the mind
Mathematical and logical certainty as model
Mind-body dualism
Systematic doubt to reach certainty
Deductive reasoning from first principles

Name: Empiricism
Description: Epistemological position that all knowledge comes from sensory experience.
Sources: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (John Locke)
A Treatise of Human Nature (David Hume)
The Principles of Human Knowledge (George Berkeley)
CorePrinciples: All knowledge derives from experience
Mind is a 'blank slate' (tabula rasa) at birth
No innate ideas
Observation and experiment as sources of knowledge
Skepticism about knowledge beyond experience
Inductive reasoning from particulars to generals
Focus on sensory perception

Name: Phenomenology
Description: Philosophical movement studying consciousness and the structures of experience from the first-person point of view.
CorePrinciples: Study of lived experience and consciousness
Intentionality: consciousness is always 'of' something
Bracketing (epoché): suspending assumptions about reality
Essence is found through phenomenological reduction
Being-in-the-world
Embodied consciousness
'To the things themselves' - return to direct experience

Name: Platonism
Description: Philosophy founded by Plato positing that abstract Forms or Ideas are the most real things, and the material world is merely an imperfect reflection of these eternal archetypes.
CorePrinciples: Theory of Forms: Abstract ideals are more real than material objects
Allegory of the Cave: Most people mistake shadows for reality
Philosopher-kings: The wise should govern society
Anamnesis: Knowledge is recollection of the Forms from before birth
Immortality of the soul
The Good as the highest Form, source of being and truth
Mathematics as bridge between material and ideal worlds
Tripartite soul: reason, spirit, appetite

Name: Epicureanism
Description: Hellenistic philosophy teaching that pleasure (specifically ataraxia — tranquility — and aponia — freedom from pain) is the highest good, achieved through simple living, friendship, and philosophical reflection.
CorePrinciples: Ataraxia: Tranquility and freedom from mental disturbance as the highest good
Aponia: Absence of bodily pain
Hedonism: Pleasure is good, pain is bad, but prudence guides choices
Friendship is the greatest external good
Death is nothing to fear: 'When death is, I am not; when I am, death is not'
Atoms and void: materialist cosmology
Withdrawal from politics for the serene life
Simple pleasures over intense but risky ones

Name: Cynicism
Description: Radical ancient Greek philosophy rejecting social conventions, wealth, and power in favor of virtue alone and living in agreement with nature.
Sources: Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers (Diogenes Laërtius)
Fragments attributed to Diogenes of Sinope
CorePrinciples: Virtue is the only true good; conventional goods (wealth, power, honor) are worthless
Live according to nature and reason, not social convention
Anaideia: Shamelessness; rejection of social norms that are contrary to virtue
Askesis: Rigorous training and self-discipline
Cosmopolitanism: Citizen of the world, not of a city-state
Freedom from desire and attachment
Critique of power, luxury, and civilization

Name: Skepticism (Pyrrhonian)
Era: 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE; modern revival
Description: Philosophical tradition advocating suspension of judgment on all matters of fact, leading to ataraxia (tranquility) through freedom from the anxiety of unresolvable beliefs.
CorePrinciples: Epoché: Suspension of judgment about all claims
No proposition can be proven with certainty
For every argument, an equal and opposite argument exists (isostheneia)
Appearances are all we have; the nature of things is hidden
Suspension of judgment leads to ataraxia (peace of mind)
Conformity with custom and appearances allows practical life
Radical questioning of all certainty

Name: Scholasticism
Description: Medieval philosophical and theological method combining Aristotelian logic with Christian doctrine, attempting to reconcile faith and reason through systematic argumentation.
Sources: Works of Duns Scotus and William of Ockham
CorePrinciples: Faith and reason are complementary, not contradictory
Aristotelian logic as tool for theological inquiry
Natural theology: reason can demonstrate some truths about God
Universal concepts are real (realism) or merely names (nominalism)
Hierarchical reality: God, angels, humans, nature
Teleological universe: everything has a divinely appointed purpose
Synthesis of Greek philosophy with Christian revelation

Name: Social Contract Theory
Description: Political philosophy proposing that legitimate political authority arises from an agreement among individuals to form a society and submit to governance in exchange for protection of their rights.
CorePrinciples: Natural state of humans before society (state of nature)
Social contract as the foundation of legitimate authority
Consent of the governed as the basis of political obligation
Rights precede and constrain government power
Veil of ignorance (Rawls): justice principles chosen without knowing one's position
Original position: fair principles arise when self-interest is removed
Government accountability to the people it governs

Name: Postmodernism
Description: Philosophical and cultural movement skeptical of grand narratives, objective truth, and foundational claims, emphasizing language, power, and the constructed nature of reality.
CorePrinciples: Incredulity toward metanarratives: no single story explains everything
Truth is constructed, not discovered; context-dependent
Deconstruction: texts contain multiple conflicting meanings
Power/knowledge: truth claims serve power structures
No fixed meaning in texts; reader creates meaning
Identity is fluid and culturally constructed
Simulation and hyperreality: copies replace originals
Critique of Enlightenment rationalism and progress

Name: Analytic Philosophy
Description: Philosophical tradition emphasizing logical analysis, clarity of language, and rigorous argumentation as the primary tools for resolving philosophical problems.
CorePrinciples: Clarity and precision in language as philosophical method
Logical analysis of propositions and arguments
Philosophy continuous with science, not opposed to it
Metaphysical claims must be verifiable or logically necessary (early positivism)
Ordinary language philosophy: problems dissolve under analysis
Reductionism: complex phenomena explained by simpler components
Formal logic as core tool for philosophy

Name: Marxist Philosophy (Dialectical Materialism)
Description: Philosophical framework combining Hegelian dialectics with materialism, positing that history is driven by class struggle and material conditions, not ideas.
CorePrinciples: Material conditions determine consciousness ('being determines consciousness')
Dialectical process: thesis-antithesis-synthesis drives change
Class struggle as the engine of historical change
Alienation: workers estranged from labor, products, species-being
Base and superstructure: economic base shapes cultural/political institutions
Ideology serves ruling class interests
Communism as the resolution of historical contradictions
Praxis: unity of theory and practice
Regions: Global influence (Soviet Union, China, Latin America, academia)

Name: Feminist Philosophy
Description: Philosophical tradition examining gender, power, and oppression, arguing that philosophical frameworks have historically excluded and marginalized women and other groups.
Sources: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Mary Wollstonecraft)
CorePrinciples: Patriarchy as a systemic structure of power, not natural order
Gender is socially constructed, not biologically determined
Standpoint epistemology: perspective shapes knowledge
Intersectionality: multiple systems of oppression interact
Care ethics: relationships and context in moral reasoning
Feminist critique of objectivity as disguised male perspective
Liberation requires structural transformation, not just individual change

Name: Nietzschean Philosophy
Description: Philosophy of Friedrich Nietzsche critiquing conventional morality, championing life-affirmation, the will to power, and the creation of new values beyond traditional good and evil.
Sources: On the Genealogy of Morality (Friedrich Nietzsche)
CorePrinciples: Death of God: traditional religious and moral frameworks have collapsed
Will to Power: fundamental drive of all life to expand and overcome
Übermensch: the ideal of self-overcoming and value creation
Eternal Recurrence: live as if every moment repeats infinitely
Slave morality vs. master morality: resentment vs. self-affirmation
Perspectivism: no objective facts, only interpretations
Amor fati: love of fate, embracing all of life
Critique of nihilism while recognizing its danger

Name: Process Philosophy
Description: Philosophical tradition holding that reality is fundamentally dynamic, relational, and processual rather than static and substance-based.
CorePrinciples: Reality is constituted by events and processes, not static substances
All actualities are 'occasions of experience'
God is not omnipotent but persuasive, luring the world toward beauty
Panpsychism: experience is a fundamental feature of all reality
Creativity as the ultimate metaphysical category
Interdependence and relationality of all things
Becoming is more fundamental than being

Name: Philosophy of Mind (Functionalism/Physicalism)
Description: Philosophical inquiry into the nature of consciousness, mental states, and the relationship between mind and body, with major positions including functionalism, physicalism, and dualism.
CorePrinciples: Mind-body problem: how does consciousness relate to physical brain?
Physicalism: mental states are identical to brain states
Functionalism: mental states defined by causal roles, not substance
Qualia and the 'hard problem': explaining subjective experience
Eliminative materialism: folk psychology is a failed theory
Dualism: mind and body are distinct substances (minority view)
Emergentism: consciousness emerges from physical complexity

Name: Environmental Ethics
Description: Branch of ethics examining the moral relationship between humans and the natural environment, including questions of animal rights, biodiversity, and obligations to future generations.
Sources: The Case for Animal Rights (Tom Regan)
CorePrinciples: Intrinsic value of nature beyond utility to humans
Moral considerability extends to animals, species, ecosystems
Land ethic: Humans are members of the biotic community, not masters
Obligations to future generations
Animal rights: sentient beings have rights not to be harmed
Anthropocentrism vs. ecocentrism as competing frameworks
Sustainability and intergenerational justice
